questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-5y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-5$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-5t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{3t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-5t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{-5t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, the only phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

\

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/f69ae5c2aeaa84d0e1b9b58da90ec738bf47a8f3c69145b990e12f13e25503e7.png)

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above.
Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?
questions.worked_solution:
Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must also approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}>0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}>0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}>0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=7y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=7y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=7$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{7t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{3t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{7t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{7t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/96801605aa5d777eb18c13ded1f7b7e59ae74968b210da3b7a26f339a1c9f673.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{3t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{7t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{7t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{3t})^{′}}=\frac{7{c}_{2}{e}^{7t}}{3{c}_{1}{e}^{3t}}=\frac{7{c}_{2}}{3{c}_{1}}{e}^{4t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to \pm \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more vertical as we move away from the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/20ef7519d0ca517d0d7d06d2998f7bd6c77f04145243f721e197fbef5c087791.png)

questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-3$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{-2t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{-3t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{-2t})^{′}}=\frac{-3{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}}{-2{c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}}=\frac{3{c}_{2}}{2{c}_{1}}{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form

lie on the $x$-axis and move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=1$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis and also move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{an unstable node (source)}.$

Let's consider the solutions $x(t) = c_1e^{-t}$ and $y(t)=c_2e^{-4t}$ provided that $c_1,c_2 \neq 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{-4t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{-t})^{′}}=\frac{-4{c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}}{-{c}_{1}{e}^{-t}}=\frac{4{c}_{2}}{{c}_{1}}{e}^{-3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as the trajectories approach the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/6c3af2fe68c4bcddbbfd9f13eb84e73014511374c0adc570084f9c92773d31e0.png)

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Classifying Decoupled Systems of Linear Differential Equations
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=4y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Interpret the stability of the $x$-axis, the $y$-axis, and the equilibrium point (the origin) for the given decoupled system of linear differential equations.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/7f53fdda091242e4fee1edd70a7e96c649eff8bac93fcdc9fed6da38ec5c7523.png)
where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/3b9909cba711a2394b8dbcda4b9d72ffbd9d37bd24b90506ac22b44c4cd398c4.png)

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue $\lambda_1=2$ with the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/1ea46da3e9697ee89d1112dfec53457657271c391a28a6c55267da70d38157c4.png) The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/9725d696549426d16093b7cd0e9bb188589472ed9ff81520c19a07ab296fb96d.png)
lie on the $x$-axis and move away from the origin as $t \to \infty.$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{unstable}}$ line.

- Eigenvalue $\lambda_2=4$ with the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/85e8d745e2b504770815bb92ad1a151f422c941874f33840593836e78eeaacde.png) The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/2f67b02cda725daa0d0b994f3f4952065793e53ddc32260b14310f5158876f4f.png)
lie on the $y$-axis and also move away from the origin as $t \to \infty.$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{unstable}}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{an unstable node (source)}}.$ 

**Note:** The phase portrait of the system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/2b79201d15fe5d2a9896cdee09c0474b97bb933d75fcf478c6fdb37cb4d16742.png)
